q: Which novel by Harper Lee is narrated by a young girl nicknamed Scout?
note: Published in 1960, it won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction the following year.

q: Which Herman Melville novel begins with the line "Call me Ishmael"?
note: It sold poorly in Melville's lifetime and only became a classic decades after his death.

q: In which George Orwell novel are citizens warned that "Big Brother is watching you"?
note: Orwell finished it in 1948 and reportedly arrived at the title by flipping the last two digits.

q: Which Jane Austen novel follows the courtship of Elizabeth Bennet and Mr. Darcy?
note: Austen originally drafted it under the title First Impressions.

q: Which Mary Shelley novel carries the subtitle "The Modern Prometheus"?
note: She began it at eighteen, during a rainy summer at Lake Geneva when Lord Byron proposed a ghost-story contest.

q: Which F. Scott Fitzgerald novel is narrated by Nick Carraway?
note: Fitzgerald died believing it a failure; it sold modestly in his lifetime and boomed only after copies were shipped to soldiers in World War II.

q: Which Charles Dickens novel opens "It was the best of times, it was the worst of times"?
note: The two cities are London and Paris, and the story climaxes at the guillotine during the French Revolution.

q: In the novel by Cervantes, what is the name of Don Quixote's squire?
note: He is promised the governorship of an island as his reward, and eventually gets a mock version of one.

q: Which Tolstoy novel opens with the observation that all happy families are alike?
note: The line has been borrowed so often by scientists and economists that it is now known as the Anna Karenina principle.

q: Which 1897 Bram Stoker novel is told through letters, diaries and newspaper clippings kept by Jonathan Harker and his friends?
note: Stoker never visited Transylvania, and researched the setting entirely from books in English libraries.

q: Which Emily Brontë novel centres on Heathcliff and Catherine Earnshaw on the Yorkshire moors?
note: It was first published under the male pen name Ellis Bell, and was her only novel.

q: Which Aldous Huxley novel is set in a World State whose citizens are bred in hatcheries and sedated with a drug called soma?
note: The title is lifted from a line spoken by Miranda in Shakespeare's The Tempest.

q: Which J.D. Salinger novel is narrated by a teenager named Holden Caulfield?
note: Salinger spent the last fifty years of his life as a near-total recluse and published no further novels.

q: Which Victor Hugo novel follows the ex-convict Jean Valjean, pursued for years by the policeman Javert?
note: Valjean's original crime was stealing a loaf of bread to feed his sister's children.

q: Which Ray Bradbury novel about book burning takes its title from a temperature?
note: Its hero, Guy Montag, is a fireman whose job is to start fires rather than put them out.

q: Which Joseph Conrad novella follows a sailor named Marlow up an African river in search of a trader called Kurtz?
note: Francis Ford Coppola transplanted its plot to the Vietnam War for the film Apocalypse Now.

q: In Dostoevsky's Crime and Punishment, what is the name of the student who murders an old pawnbroker?
note: His surname comes from a Russian word for a schism or split, matching his divided conscience.

q: Which Thomas Hardy novel ends with its heroine arrested at Stonehenge?
note: The outcry over the book's sympathy for a "fallen woman" helped push Hardy to abandon novels for poetry.

q: In Kafka's The Metamorphosis, what is the name of the travelling salesman who wakes up transformed into a giant insect?
note: Kafka insisted his publisher never illustrate the creature on the cover.

q: What is the name of the fictional town where Gabriel García Márquez sets One Hundred Years of Solitude?
note: The novel traces seven generations of the Buendía family in that town, and helped win its author the Nobel Prize.

q: Which British author created the detective Sherlock Holmes?
note: He grew so tired of Holmes that he killed him off at the Reichenbach Falls, then revived him after a public outcry.

q: Who wrote the Harry Potter series of novels?
note: Her publisher used initials rather than her first name in the hope that boys would pick up the book.

q: Which American author wrote The Adventures of Tom Sawyer under a pen name?
note: Born Samuel Clemens, he took his pen name from a riverboat call meaning water two fathoms deep.

q: Who wrote The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings?
note: He was a professor of Anglo-Saxon at Oxford, and invented the Elvish languages before he invented the stories.

q: Which Danish writer wrote the fairy tales "The Little Mermaid" and "The Ugly Duckling"?
note: A bronze statue of his little mermaid has sat on a rock in Copenhagen harbour since 1913.

q: Which American writer wrote the poem "The Raven"?
note: The bird's single croaked word, "Nevermore", made him famous almost overnight but earned him only about nine dollars.

q: Which English poet wrote the lines beginning "I wandered lonely as a cloud"?
note: The daffodils in the poem were ones his sister Dorothy described first, in her journal.

q: Which reclusive American poet of Amherst, Massachusetts wrote "Because I could not stop for Death"?
note: Fewer than a dozen of her roughly 1,800 poems were published while she was alive.

q: Which American poet wrote "The Road Not Taken" and "Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening"?
note: He read at John F. Kennedy's inauguration, though glare off the snow forced him to recite from memory instead.

q: Which Russian writer, also a practising doctor, wrote the play The Cherry Orchard?
note: He called medicine his lawful wife and literature his mistress.

q: Which American author wrote A Farewell to Arms and The Old Man and the Sea?
note: His stripped-down style, all short declarative sentences, was shaped by his years as a newspaper reporter.

q: Which Canadian author wrote the dystopian novel The Handmaid's Tale?
note: She has said she included nothing in the book that some society had not already done somewhere.

q: Which Italian poet wrote The Divine Comedy?
note: By writing it in Tuscan rather than Latin he did more than anyone to make that dialect into modern Italian.

q: Which of the Brontë sisters wrote Jane Eyre?
note: She published it as Currer Bell, and reviewers spent months arguing about whether the author was a man.

q: Which Irish writer wrote the novel The Picture of Dorian Gray and the play The Importance of Being Earnest?
note: Earnest opened in London in 1895, at the very height of his fame and only weeks before his ruin.

q: Which Nigerian author wrote Things Fall Apart?
note: He took the title from a line in W.B. Yeats's poem "The Second Coming".

q: Which poet wrote the 1922 modernist poem "The Waste Land"?
note: Ezra Pound cut the draft roughly in half, and Eliot dedicated the poem to him in gratitude.

q: Which Argentine writer wrote the labyrinthine short-story collections Ficciones and The Aleph?
note: He went blind in middle age, around the same time he was appointed director of Argentina's national library.

q: Which Japanese noblewoman wrote The Tale of Genji, often called the world's first novel?
note: She wrote it around a thousand years ago as a lady-in-waiting at the Heian imperial court.

q: Which American poet wrote "O Captain! My Captain!", an elegy for Abraham Lincoln?
note: He spent his life expanding a single book, Leaves of Grass, through edition after edition.

q: Which Italian artist painted the Mona Lisa?
note: The painting became a worldwide celebrity partly because it was stolen from the Louvre in 1911 and missing for two years.

q: Which Dutch post-Impressionist painted The Starry Night?
note: He painted the swirling night sky from a window of the asylum at Saint-Rémy, from memory rather than direct observation.

q: Which artist painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel?
note: He considered himself a sculptor rather than a painter and took the commission reluctantly, spending four years on the scaffold.

q: Which Spanish artist painted Guernica and helped invent Cubism?
note: Guernica was his response to the bombing of a Basque town during the Spanish Civil War in 1937.

q: In which Paris museum does the Mona Lisa hang?
note: The building was a royal palace long before it became a museum, opening to the public after the French Revolution.

q: Which Norwegian artist painted The Scream?
note: He made several versions of the image, and two of them have been stolen and later recovered.

q: Which French sculptor created the bronze figure known as The Thinker?
note: The figure began as a small part of a much larger doorway sculpture, The Gates of Hell.

q: Which Spanish Surrealist painted The Persistence of Memory, with its drooping melted watches?
note: He said the soft watches were inspired by a wheel of Camembert melting in the sun.

q: Which French painter's canvas Impression, Sunrise gave the Impressionist movement its name?
note: A hostile critic coined the word "Impressionists" as an insult, and the painters cheerfully adopted it.

q: Which Mexican painter is known for unflinching self-portraits and the double portrait The Two Fridas?
note: She began painting seriously while bedridden after a streetcar accident, using a mirror mounted above her bed.

q: Which American artist painted Nighthawks, showing four figures in a late-night diner?
note: There is no visible door into the diner, which is part of why the scene feels so sealed off.

q: Which Dutch master painted the enormous militia group portrait known as The Night Watch?
note: Its familiar nickname comes from centuries of darkened varnish; the scene is actually set in daylight.

q: Which artist made the Pop Art silkscreens of Campbell's Soup Cans and Marilyn Monroe?
note: He began as a successful commercial illustrator, which is exactly why the art world was slow to take him seriously.

q: Which Italian Renaissance artist painted The Birth of Venus, showing the goddess arriving on a scallop shell?
note: It hangs in the Uffizi in Florence, painted for the Medici circle at the height of their power.

q: What is the title of Grant Wood's painting of a stern farmer holding a pitchfork beside a woman, in front of a white farmhouse?
note: The title refers to the pointed window on the house behind them, a style called Carpenter Gothic.

q: Which famous armless ancient Greek statue of Aphrodite is named after the island where it was found?
note: A farmer uncovered it on Milos in 1820, and nobody knows what the missing arms were doing.

q: Which Dutch painter created Girl with a Pearl Earring?
note: Only about three dozen paintings are firmly attributed to him, and he was largely forgotten for two centuries.

q: Which Spanish painter put himself at his easel in the royal group portrait Las Meninas?
note: The king and queen appear only as a small reflection in a mirror at the back of the room.

q: Which Japanese artist made the woodblock print The Great Wave off Kanagawa?
note: It is one sheet from his series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, and the mountain sits small behind the wave.

q: Which Netherlandish painter created the crowded, nightmarish triptych The Garden of Earthly Delights?
note: One damned figure in the hell panel has musical notation written across his backside, which modern musicians have transcribed and played.

q: Which Shakespeare play is about young lovers from the feuding Montague and Capulet families of Verona?
note: Shakespeare did not invent the plot; he reworked an English poem that was itself based on Italian tales.

q: Which Shakespeare play contains the soliloquy beginning "To be, or not to be"?
note: At around 4,000 lines it is Shakespeare's longest play, and Hamlet has more lines than any other character he wrote.

q: Which Shakespeare tragedy opens with three witches and follows a Scottish thane who murders his king?
note: Theatre superstition holds that saying its name inside a theatre is unlucky, so actors call it "the Scottish play".

q: Which Andrew Lloyd Webber musical features a masked figure living beneath the Paris Opera House?
note: It is based on a 1910 novel by the French writer Gaston Leroux.

q: What is the name of the round London playhouse associated with Shakespeare's company, rebuilt near its original site in 1997?
note: The original burned down in 1613 when a stage cannon set the thatched roof alight during a performance of Henry VIII.

q: Which Shakespeare comedy features the fairy king Oberon and a mischievous sprite named Puck?
note: Puck's other name in the play, Robin Goodfellow, comes straight out of English folk belief.

q: In Shakespeare's Julius Caesar, what warning does the soothsayer call out to Caesar in the street?
note: The Ides simply meant the middle of the month, in this case 15 March.

q: Which Shakespeare tragedy features a Moorish general destroyed by the scheming of his ensign Iago?
note: Iago speaks more lines than the title character, which is unusual for a Shakespeare villain.

q: Which Shakespeare tragedy begins with an ageing king dividing his kingdom among his daughters?
note: For roughly 150 years the play was performed only in a rewritten version with a happy ending.

q: In which Samuel Beckett play do two tramps, Vladimir and Estragon, wait by a tree for someone who never arrives?
note: Beckett wrote it in French first, then translated it into his native English himself.

q: Which Arthur Miller play dramatises the Salem witch trials?
note: Miller wrote it in 1953 as a parallel to the anti-communist hearings then gripping the United States.

q: Which Tennessee Williams play pits the fragile Blanche DuBois against her brother-in-law Stanley Kowalski?
note: The streetcar of the title was a real New Orleans line running along Desire Street.

q: Which Greek tragedy by Sophocles concerns a king who unknowingly kills his father and marries his mother?
note: Freud borrowed the king's name for his theory some 2,400 years after the play was written.

q: In The Merchant of Venice, which moneylender demands a pound of flesh as forfeit on a loan?
note: He is undone by a technicality: the bond entitles him to flesh, but not to a single drop of blood.

q: Which Shakespeare play is set on an island ruled by the exiled magician Prospero?
note: It is widely thought to be the last play he wrote alone, and Prospero's farewell to his magic is often read as Shakespeare's own.

q: What three-word phrase do theatre people traditionally use to wish a performer good luck?
note: Wishing someone plain good luck is considered a jinx, so the superstition demands you wish them harm instead.

q: Which Norwegian playwright wrote A Doll's House, which ends with Nora walking out and slamming the door?
note: German theatres of the day forced him to supply an alternative ending in which Nora stays.

q: Which fat, boastful, cowardly knight is Prince Hal's drinking companion in Shakespeare's Henry IV plays?
note: He proved so popular that Shakespeare gave him his own comedy, The Merry Wives of Windsor.

q: Which ancient Greek playwright wrote the trilogy known as the Oresteia?
note: It is the only complete trilogy to survive from Greek tragedy.

q: In Shakespeare's Twelfth Night, what name does the shipwrecked Viola take while disguised as a young man?
note: The tangle is complete when Olivia falls for the disguise and Viola falls for the duke she is serving.

q: Which German composer wrote the Ninth Symphony, with its "Ode to Joy" finale, after going deaf?
note: At the 1824 premiere he had to be turned around to see the applause he could not hear.

q: Which Austrian child prodigy composed The Magic Flute and died in 1791 at the age of 35?
note: He left his Requiem unfinished at his death, and a pupil completed it for the widow to collect the fee.

q: Which Russian composer wrote the ballets Swan Lake and The Nutcracker?
note: The Nutcracker was a flop at its 1892 premiere and only became a Christmas fixture much later.

q: Which Italian composer wrote the set of violin concertos known as The Four Seasons?
note: He was an ordained priest with red hair, nicknamed the Red Priest, who taught music at a Venetian orphanage for girls.

q: Which German composer wrote the Brandenburg Concertos and the Goldberg Variations?
note: He fathered twenty children, and several of his sons became famous composers in their own right.

q: Which section of a symphony orchestra contains the violins, violas, cellos and double basses?
note: It is by far the largest section, and its players are the only ones who normally all play the same few instrument types.

q: Which Puccini opera is set in Nagasaki and centres on a young Japanese bride called Cio-Cio-San?
note: It was booed off the stage at its 1904 premiere at La Scala; Puccini revised it and it became one of the most performed operas ever written.

q: Which Italian composer wrote the operas Rigoletto, La Traviata and Aida?
note: Aida was written for a grand opera house in Cairo, and premiered there in 1871.

q: Which German composer wrote the four-opera Ring cycle, which includes the "Ride of the Valkyries"?
note: He had an entire theatre built at Bayreuth to his own specifications just to stage the cycle properly.

q: Which composer wrote the Water Music and the oratorio Messiah, with its "Hallelujah" chorus?
note: German-born, he settled in London and became a British subject, and is buried in Westminster Abbey.

q: Which Polish-born composer wrote almost exclusively for solo piano, including a famous set of nocturnes and mazurkas?
note: He spent his adult life in Paris and asked that his heart be returned to Warsaw after his death, which it was.

q: Which composer's ballet The Rite of Spring caused a near-riot at its 1913 Paris premiere?
note: The jagged choreography upset the audience as much as the music, and the dancers had to take their counts shouted from the wings.

q: What Italian musical term describes the speed at which a piece is played?
note: The word simply means "time" in Italian, the language that supplied most of Western music's performance vocabulary.

q: Which Austrian composer of more than a hundred symphonies is nicknamed the "Father of the Symphony"?
note: He taught the young Beethoven and was a close friend of Mozart, bridging two generations of Viennese music.

q: In opera, what name is given to the highest female voice type?
note: The word comes from the Italian for "above", since the part sits on top of the vocal texture.

q: Which French composer wrote the opera Carmen?
note: He died a few months after its cool reception in 1875, never knowing it would become one of the most popular operas in the world.

q: Which composer wrote the tone poem Also sprach Zarathustra, whose sunrise opening was used in the film 2001: A Space Odyssey?
note: He was no relation to the Viennese waltz Strausses, a confusion that followed him all his life.

q: Which Russian composer wrote the piano suite Pictures at an Exhibition?
note: He wrote it in memory of a friend, an artist whose drawings the movements depict, and Ravel's later orchestration made it a concert staple.

q: Which Czech composer wrote the symphony known as "From the New World" while living in the United States?
note: He was running a New York conservatory at the time and urged American composers to build on their own folk traditions.

q: Which Victorian writing-and-composing partnership produced the comic operas The Mikado and The Pirates of Penzance?
note: Gilbert wrote the words and Sullivan the music, and the two men quarrelled bitterly for years over, among other things, a carpet.

q: In Greek mythology, which god rules the other gods from Mount Olympus?
note: The Romans identified him with Jupiter, and his weapon in both traditions is the thunderbolt.

q: Which Paris landmark was built as the entrance arch for the 1889 World's Fair?
note: It was meant to be dismantled after twenty years and survived mainly because it made such a useful radio mast.

q: In Greek mythology, which hero's only vulnerable spot was his heel?
note: His mother dipped him in the river Styx as a baby but held him by the heel, leaving that patch untouched.

q: Which white marble mausoleum at Agra in India was built by an emperor as a tomb for his wife?
note: Shah Jahan built it for Mumtaz Mahal, who died giving birth to their fourteenth child.

q: In Norse mythology, which hammer-wielding god is associated with thunder?
note: His hammer is called Mjölnir, and Thursday is named after him.

q: In Greek myth, what half-man, half-bull creature was kept in the Labyrinth on Crete?
note: Theseus killed it and found his way back out using a thread given to him by Ariadne.

q: In Greek myth, who ignored his father's warning and flew so close to the sun that his wax wings melted?
note: His father Daedalus, who built the wings, also designed the Labyrinth they were escaping from.

q: Which Roman god corresponds to the Greek god of war, Ares?
note: The Romans thought far better of him than the Greeks did of Ares, treating him as a founding father of Rome itself.

q: Which Spanish architect designed the Sagrada Família church in Barcelona?
note: He worked on it for more than forty years and knew he would never see it finished; construction is still going on.

q: What is the name of the great oval amphitheatre in Rome, completed around AD 80?
note: Its formal name was the Flavian Amphitheatre, after the emperors who built it, and it held roughly 50,000 spectators.

q: In Greek myth, what one thing remained inside Pandora's box after everything else had escaped?
note: It was originally a large storage jar; "box" crept in through a mistranslation in the sixteenth century.

q: Which American architect designed the spiral-ramped Guggenheim Museum in New York and the house called Fallingwater?
note: He died a few months before the Guggenheim opened in 1959, after sixteen years of wrangling over the design.

q: In Greek myth, which musician was allowed to lead his wife Eurydice out of the underworld provided he did not look back?
note: He looked back within sight of daylight, and the story has been set as an opera more often than almost any other myth.

q: Which ancient temple dedicated to Athena stands on the Acropolis in Athens?
note: It stood largely intact for over two thousand years until a Venetian shell hit the gunpowder stored inside it in 1687.

q: In Norse mythology, what name is given to the prophesied final battle in which many of the gods die?
note: Wagner borrowed it for the last opera of his Ring cycle, under the German name Götterdämmerung.

q: Which style of architecture is defined by pointed arches, ribbed vaults and flying buttresses, as seen in Notre-Dame de Paris?
note: Renaissance critics coined the name as an insult, meaning barbarian work fit for Goths.

q: Which Danish architect designed the Sydney Opera House?
note: He won the competition in 1957, resigned in a funding row before the building was finished, and never saw it completed in person.

q: In Greek myth, which hero beheaded the Gorgon Medusa?
note: He avoided her petrifying gaze by watching her reflection in a polished shield.

q: What name is given to the thousands of life-size clay soldiers buried near the tomb of China's first emperor?
note: Farmers digging a well near Xi'an stumbled on them in 1974, more than two thousand years after they were buried.

q: In Norse mythology, what is the name of the great tree whose branches and roots link the nine worlds?
note: It is usually described as an ash, with a serpent gnawing at its roots and an eagle perched at the top.
